## Where we are

- This seminar is about **how complex words get built while you are talking**.

::: {.fragment}
- Before we can ask that, we need the piece everybody already agrees on: how a
  *single, simple* word gets out of your mouth.
:::

::: {.fragment}
- Today's reading is the map. The rest of the semester is us arguing about one
  corner of it.
:::

::: {.fragment .aside}
It is a handbook chapter, so it is a list of facts, not an argument. Read it as
a checklist: "any model I ever propose has to explain these."
:::

::: footer
Course schedule, Week 1
:::

## Today's goals

Our discussion today will touch on:

- The three-step picture of speaking
- Why *choosing a word* and *building its sounds* are two different steps
- Properties 1--9: the fact, and the evidence behind the fact
- Where function words and morphemes fit --- and why that is our whole course

## Speaking is not listening, reversed

- Recognizing a word in your native language is fast, automatic, and needs no
  intention.
- Producing the *same* word needs an intention and takes up to five times longer.

::: {.fragment}
::: {.claim}
Listeners start looking at the referent **before** the speaker has finished
saying the word. Speakers need about **900 ms** to start naming a pictured
object.
:::
:::

::: {.fragment .aside}
So the first thing to give up: production is its own system, with its own
problems.
:::

::: footer
Tanenhaus et al. 1995; Snodgrass & Yuditsky 1996
:::

## Two warnings before we start

- Almost everything in this chapter is about **single, isolated utterances**.
  Conversation, narrative, turn-taking: all real, all set aside.
- Almost everything is about **nouns**. Some verbs. Nothing else.

::: {.fragment .prompt}
Keep asking, all semester: does this result survive if the word is longer than
one morpheme? If it is not a noun?
:::

::: footer
Levelt 1989; Clark 1996; Ferreira & Englehart, this volume
:::

## The three steps

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
- **Conceptualization** --- decide what to express
- **Formulation** --- decide how to express it
- **Articulation** --- say it
:::
::: {.column width="55%"}
![](figs/fig1-stages.png)
:::
::::

::: footer
Levelt 1989; Figure 1, Griffin & Ferreira 2006:22
:::

## Formulation splits in two

- **Word selection.** Pick an item from your vocabulary that fits the meaning
  *and* the syntactic context. That item is the **lemma**.
- **Sound processing.** Retrieve the segments, build syllables and stress
  (*phonological encoding*), then specify motor programs (*phonetic encoding*).

::: {.fragment}
::: {.claim}
A lemma is not a sound and not a concept. It is the thing that knows *"there is
a word for this, and it is a count noun."*
:::
:::

::: footer
Fromkin 1971; Garrett 1975; Kempen & Huijbers 1983
:::

## The chapter is a list of properties

- Property 1 --- the steps
- Properties 2--9 --- from meaning to word ← **we stop here**
- Properties 10--13 --- assembling the sounds
- Properties 14--15 --- how it all plays out in time

::: {.fragment .aside}
Models disagree less than you would expect. They mostly agree on the facts and
differ on the mechanism, and on which stage they bothered to model.
:::

# 1.1 Word selection precedes sound assembly

## Property 1

::: {.claim}
Speakers access words by meaning first, then work on the sounds.
:::

Two kinds of evidence:

::: {.fragment}
1. **Speech errors** come in types, and the types line up with the steps.
2. **Time course** in picture--word interference.
:::

::: footer
Fromkin 1971; Garrett 1975
:::

## Errors come in types {.smaller}

| Error type | Example |
|---|---|
| Semantic word substitution | "give him the **yel**- er the **pink** ... the *green* jersey" |
| Blend | "**Justi:ce**, *Justin and Travis*" |
| Phonological word substitution | "the battle for the green **journey** [*jersey*]" |
| Morpheme substitution | "an awful lot of use**less** information. use*FUL* information" |
| Sound substitution | "the **raid**-- uh . the *roadie* is accepting..." |


::: footer
Table 1, Griffin & Ferreira 2006:24
:::

## Errors come in types

::: {.aside}
Most of the examples in Table 1 come from one cycling commentator at the 2005
Tour de France. Talking fast for six hours a day is very good for error corpora.
:::

- Corpora like this are **opportunistic**. You get what people happen to say.
- The rates are low: roughly 2.5 word errors and 1.5 sound errors per 10,000
  words of running speech.

::: {.fragment .prompt}
Which errors do you think are *undercollected*, and why would that matter?
:::

::: footer
Deese 1984; Fromkin 1971
:::

## Why the types matter

::: {.fragment}
- You can pick the **wrong word** and pronounce it perfectly.
:::
::: {.fragment}
- You can pick the **right word** and scramble its sounds.
:::
::: {.fragment}
- Those are two different failures, so there are two different steps.
:::

::: {.fragment .prompt}
Notice the fourth row. *Morphemes* substitute too, and they substitute
separately from the stem. Hold onto that one.
:::

## Picture--word interference

::: {.todo}
PLACEHOLDER --- schematic of the paradigm.

Picture of a lion + distractor word, distractor appearing at SOA
−400 / −200 / 0 / +200 ms. Task: name the picture, ignore the word.
:::

::: footer
Schriefers, Meyer & Levelt 1990
:::

## Picture--word interference: the pattern

- **Semantically** related distractor (*tiger* while naming a lion):
  **slows** naming, when it comes at or before the picture.
- **Phonologically** related distractor (*liar* while naming a lion):
  **speeds** naming, when it comes at or after the picture.

::: {.fragment}
Opposite directions, and opposite points in time.
:::

::: {.fragment .aside}
Griffin & Ferreira are careful here, and you should be too: reading the
distractor is comprehension, so every interpretation of this paradigm rests on
assumptions about how comprehension and production interact.
:::

::: footer
Glaser & Düngelhoff 1984; Damian & Martin 1999; Starreveld 2000
:::

## What Property 1 buys the models

- Two stages, and two separate levels of representation: word-level and
  sound-level.

::: {.fragment}
::: {.claim}
There is no route from meaning to sounds that skips the word.
:::
:::

::: footer
Caramazza 1997; Dell 1986; Levelt et al. 1999
:::

# 1.2 Selecting a content word

## Property 2: one intention wakes a family

- Semantic substitutions: calling a van *bus*.
- Blends: *behavior* + *deportment* → **behortment**.

::: {.fragment}
::: {.claim}
Getting to a word from a meaning is not surgical. You activate a neighbourhood.
:::
:::

::: {.fragment}
Which raises the obvious question: what *is* a meaning, in these models?
:::

::: footer
Dell et al. 1997; Garrett 1975; Wells 1951/1973
:::

## Two answers about meaning

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Non-decompositional**

`BIRD` is one atomic lexical concept.

Neighbours come from links in a network: `BIRD` → `ANIMAL` → `FISH` → *fish*.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Decompositional**

`bird` = HAS WINGS, HAS FEATHERS, SINGS SONGS.

Neighbours come from shared features: airplanes have wings, opera singers sing.
:::
::::

::: footer
Fodor 1975; Roelofs 1992; Levelt et al. 1999 (left) --- Dell 1986; Vigliocco et al. 2004 (right)
:::

## Two answers about meaning

![](figs/fig2-models.png){width="78%"}

::: footer
Figure 2, Griffin & Ferreira 2006:27. WEAVER++ (Levelt et al. 1999) left, Dell et al. (1997) right.
:::

## Two answers about meaning

- Decompositional gets similarity for free: overlap in features.
- Non-decompositional has to build similarity out of network links.
- Both have to explain why the neighbourhood is **context-dependent** ---
  blends only involve words that are interchangeable *in that sentence*.

::: {.fragment .prompt}
For us: if a morpheme carries meaning, which of these two boxes does *-ed* go
in? Does `PAST` have features?
:::

::: footer
Garrett 1975; Levelt 1989
:::

## Property 3: similar meanings compete

- Words that intrude in substitutions share grammatical class, taxonomic
  category, and level of specificity with the target.
- Related distractors slow you down relative to unrelated ones.

::: {.fragment}
::: {.claim}
But *dog* and *bone* do not compete. Association is not enough. It has to be
**similarity of meaning**.
:::
:::

::: footer
Fromkin 1971; Nooteboom 1973
:::

## How models make words compete

- **Activation only.** Probability of selection tracks activation. Enough for
  error patterns, not enough for latencies.
- **Lateral inhibition.** The more active a word is, the harder it pushes the
  others down. Time-to-threshold is your reaction time.
- **WEAVER++.** Two factors: a ratio of the target's activation to everything
  else in the response set, plus a **critical difference** the target has to
  clear.

::: {.fragment}
::: {.aside}
That last one makes a real prediction: one strong competitor is worse than two
half-strength ones.
:::
:::

::: footer
Dell 1986; Cutting & Ferreira 1999; Harley 1993; Levelt et al. 1999; Luce 1959
:::

## Property 3, a small case: codability

- *tooth*, *bomb*: one dominant name → fast.
- *TV / television*, *weights / barbells*: two good names → slow.

::: {.fragment}
The second name is a competitor you brought with you.
:::

::: footer
Lachman 1973; Lachman, Shaffer & Hennrikus 1974
:::

## Property 4: fenced in by grammatical class

- Nouns substitute for nouns, verbs for verbs.
- Distractors interfere when they share grammatical class, verb transitivity,
  and other context-relevant syntactic features.
- Even purely *phonological* substitutions tend to keep the category.

::: {.fragment}
::: {.claim}
The pressure to keep the grammatical class is **stronger** than the pressure to
keep the meaning.
:::
:::

::: {.fragment .aside}
This is the first place syntax enters the model, and it enters as a frame with
slots: a noun slot only accepts nouns.
:::

::: footer
Fromkin 1971; Garrett 1975; Schriefers 1993; Fay & Cutler 1977
:::

## Property 5: which meanings are easy

- **Imageability / concreteness.** *vampire, wind, pine* beat *fear, sense,
  spirit*.
- **Predictability.** The more predictable a word is in context, the fewer
  pauses and *um*s before it, and the faster the naming.

::: {.fragment}
::: {.claim}
The twist: imageable words are produced faster **and** are more likely to be
replaced by a semantically related word.
:::
:::

::: {.fragment .aside}
Richer meaning helps you find the word, and gives you more neighbours to trip
over.
:::

::: footer
Morrison et al. 1997; De Groot 1989, 1992; Griffin & Bock 1998; Goldman-Eisler 1958
:::

## Property 6: looking is not naming

- Distractor **word** *banana* while you say *apple* → interference.
- Distractor **picture** of a banana while you say *apple* → **facilitation**.

::: {.fragment}
::: {.claim}
Words seem to get activated only when you intend to talk about the thing.
Objects on their own do not push you into the lexicon.
:::
:::

::: {.fragment .aside}
Speakers even look right at an object while deliberately naming it wrong
(Griffin & Oppenheimer 2003).
:::

::: footer
Bloem & La Heij 2003; Damian & Bowers 2003
:::

## Property 6: except it is not clean

- Ignored objects show **no** semantic interference...
- ...but they *do* speed you up when their name sounds like your target
  (*cap* while naming a *cat*).

::: {.fragment}
::: {.claim}
Every model routes phonology through the word. So if you got phonology from the
ignored object, the word was active. And then where is the semantic
interference?
:::
:::

::: {.fragment .prompt}
Open problem. Good place for a question.
:::

::: footer
Morsella & Miozzo 2002; Navarrete & Costa 2005
:::

## Property 7: selection leaves a trace

- Repetition priming for object naming lasts **months**.
- Perseveration: name a zebra, then call the giraffe *zebra*.
- Semantic homogeneity: naming many animals in a row gets slower.

::: {.fragment}
- None of this happens if you just read the word aloud or categorize it. You
  have to **select** it from a meaning.
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.claim}
Reading, phonological assembly, and sentence production all have learning
models. Word production does not. The authors name this as a gap.
:::
:::

::: footer
Cave 1997; Bartram 1974; Vitkovitch & Humphreys 1991; Vigliocco et al. 2002
:::

## Property 8: stopping halfway

Tip-of-the-tongue. You have the word and you cannot say it.

::: {.fragment}
What you still know in a TOT state:

- its first letter or sound, its number of syllables, words it rhymes with
- whether it is count or mass in English
- its grammatical gender in Italian or French
- which auxiliary the verb takes in Italian
:::

::: footer
Brown & McNeill 1966; Burke et al. 1991
:::

## Property 8: what TOTs buy us

- **WEAVER++.** The lemma was selected --- that is why you know the syntax ---
  and retrieval of the **lexeme** failed.
- **Node Structure Theory.** No lexeme. A lexical node fails to fully activate
  phonology because the connections are weak.
- Anomia after brain damage looks the same: gender preserved, form gone.

::: {.fragment}
::: {.claim}
This is the cleanest single argument that the lemma and the form are separate
things.
:::
:::

::: footer
Levelt et al. 1999; MacKay 1987; Badecker, Miozzo & Zanuttini 1995
:::

# 1.3 Function words and morphemes

## Property 9: not selected by meaning

Articles, determiners, *-ed*. Their form depends on the **neighbours**, not on
the message.

::: {.ex}
(1)&nbsp;&nbsp; a noodle / some pasta &nbsp;&nbsp;<span class="gloss">(count vs. mass, English)</span>

(2)&nbsp;&nbsp; ett bord 'a table' / en stol 'a chair' &nbsp;&nbsp;<span class="gloss">(gender, Swedish)</span>

(3)&nbsp;&nbsp; mon chapeau, mon arbre / ma table, mon ampoule &nbsp;&nbsp;<span class="gloss">(gender + phonology, French)</span>
:::

::: {.fragment .aside}
The French case is the interesting one: *ampoule* is feminine but takes *mon*,
because the next sound decides.
:::

::: footer
Janssen & Caramazza 2003
:::

## Property 9: the experimental handle

Dutch. Naming *het groene huis* 'the green house'.

::: {.fragment}
- Distractor *been* 'leg' --- also takes *het* → faster.
- Distractor *tafel* 'table' --- takes *de* → **slower**.
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.claim}
The determiner's form is competing, and the competition is over a
**grammatical** feature of a word you are not even saying.
:::
:::

::: {.fragment .aside}
Schriefers et al. 2002/2005 is our Week 8. This is the seed of it.
:::

::: footer
Schriefers 1993
:::

## Property 9: two more facts

- In **agrammatic aphasia**, function word production is badly impaired ---
  even though function words are the most frequent and phonologically simplest
  things in the language.
- Function words participate in **speech errors** differently from content
  words.

::: footer
Bates, Wulfeck & MacWhinney 1991; Dell 1990; Garrett 1975; Stemberger 1985
:::

## Property 9: two accounts

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Positional frames**

Function words are built into the frame that content words get slotted into.
Retrieving them is part of syntactic encoding, not lexical selection.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Indirect election**

You retrieve the content word first. The content word's syntactic knowledge then
triggers retrieval of the function words it licenses.
:::
::::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.claim}
Both say the same negative thing: a function word is not retrieved by its
meaning. It is retrieved through the syntax of something else.
:::
:::

::: footer
Garrett 1975; Levelt 1989; Ferreira 2000
:::

# Why we started here

## Property 9 is the whole course

- The chapter has a big, careful section on **content words**, and one page for
  **everything else**.
- "Everything else" is where we live: *-ed*, *-lAr*, compounds, prefix stacks,
  suspended affixation.

::: {.fragment .prompt}
Three questions to carry:

1. Is *-ed* really in the same box as *the*?
2. Is a compound one selection or two?
3. If Distributed Morphology is right and words are **built by syntax**, what
   happens to a stage called "word selection"?
:::

::: footer
Course description
:::

## Key takeaways

1. Meaning first, sounds second, and never a shortcut between them.
2. Selection is competitive, and the competition is over **similar meanings**
   inside the **same grammatical class**.
3. The word can succeed while its form fails. That is a TOT.
4. Function words and morphemes get a different, syntax-driven route.
5. The models mostly agree on the facts. They differ on the mechanism.

## What the rest of the chapter does

We are not reading this, but so you know it is there:

- **§1.4** Sounds are assembled **anew** every time; experience makes it faster;
  it goes left to right; phonological neighbours help sometimes and hurt others.
- **§1.5** Timing: semantic competitors activate their own sounds, and how far
  ahead you plan in a multi-word utterance.

::: {.fragment}
Thursday we keep going on production, and then Levelt (1989) Ch. 9 next week.
:::

::: footer
Griffin & Ferreira 2006, §1.4--§2
:::

## Bring questions

::: {.prompt}
- Property 1 says meaning-based selection comes first. What would a result look
  like that **broke** that? Would you believe it?
- Property 3 says similarity competes and association does not. Are *bake* and
  *cake* similar, associated, or neither?
- Property 6: how would you tell "the word was never activated" apart from "the
  word was activated and then suppressed"?
- Property 9: pick a morpheme in a language you know whose form depends on its
  neighbours. Which of the two accounts handles it better?
:::
